title: Drug-induced photosensitivity
summary: Many common drugs make the skin burn or react in sunlight. Phototoxic reactions look like exaggerated sunburn; photoallergic ones look like eczema. A medication review is the key intervention.

glance.think: Exaggerated sunburn, blistering, eczema or pigment change on sun-exposed skin after starting a drug (doxycycline, thiazides, amiodarone, NSAIDs, quinine, voriconazole).
glance.engine: Phototoxic: the drug absorbs UVA and directly damages skin (dose-dependent). Photoallergic: UV turns the drug into an allergen (type IV).
glance.backbone: Review and stop or switch the culprit where possible, counsel UVA protection, treat with cool compresses and potent topical steroid; Yellow Card.
glance.never_miss: Voriconazole-related SCC risk, and lupus or pellagra as differentials.

what: An abnormal skin reaction to UV (mostly **UVA, 320–400 nm**) or visible light caused by a **systemic or topical drug** (or chemical). Two mechanisms: **phototoxic** (common; non-immune) and **photoallergic** (uncommon; immune). Some drugs do both. A core pharmacist topic because most cases follow a medicine started in the previous days–months, and many are preventable with counselling at the point of supply.

list: **Dose- and light-dose-dependent**; can happen to **anyone, on first exposure**, no sensitisation needed.

Requires **prior sensitisation**, only affects a minority, not strictly dose-related; may cross-react with chemically related drugs and may **persist** after drug withdrawal (persistent light reaction → CAD). Topical agents (ketoprofen gel, sunscreen filters, fragrances, phenothiazine creams) are commoner causes than oral drugs.

head: Feature
Phototoxic
Photoallergic
rows: **Exaggerated sunburn**: erythema, oedema, blistering, then hyperpigmentation/desquamation; may cause photo-onycholysis (tetracyclines, psoralens), slate-grey pigmentation (amiodarone), pseudoporphyria
**Sharply limited to exposed skin**, clear cut-off (watch strap, collar, T-shirt)
Exposed skin **and can spread to covered sites**
**Tetracyclines (doxycycline)**, fluoroquinolones, NSAIDs (oral), amiodarone, thiazides, voriconazole, psoralens, chlorpromazine, St John's wort
Topical **ketoprofen**, sunscreen filters (benzophenones/oxybenzone, octocrylene), fragrance (musk ambrette), sulfonamides, phenothiazines, quinine/quinidine, thiazides (both)

features: (Tutor's three discriminators: sensitisation, distribution, burning vs itching.)

Other drug-related photo-patterns: **drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus** (thiazides, terbinafine, PPIs, calcium-channel blockers, checkpoint inhibitors), **drug-induced pellagra** (isoniazid), **lichenoid photo-eruption** (thiazides, quinine), **methotrexate UV-recall** of a recent sunburn.
diagnosis: Clinical + **temporal drug history** (including OTC, topical, herbal — St John's wort — and supplements, and recent dose increases). Specialist: **phototesting on and off the drug**, **photopatch testing** for suspected photoallergens, biopsy if lupus/lichenoid suspected; ANA/Ro if lupus-like.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Proportionate to exposure; no new drug
Papular, recurrent seasonal, no drug link
Bizarre streaks/drips where plant/juice touched; no drug

list: **Identify and stop/switch the culprit** where possible, in discussion with the original prescriber (e.g. doxycycline → lymecycline is also a tetracycline, so consider a non-tetracycline per indication; thiazide → alternative antihypertensive). **Never stop amiodarone, voriconazole or antiretroviral/oncology drugs without specialist input** — manage with photoprotection instead; amiodarone photosensitivity can persist for months after stopping.

**Acute phototoxic reaction:** cool compresses, emollients, analgesia (paracetamol; avoid if NSAID is the culprit), **potent topical corticosteroid** short course for inflammation on body; burn-type dressings for blisters; oral antihistamine for itch.

**Prevention:** counsel at supply, especially before holidays: broad-spectrum high-UVA sunscreen, cover up, avoid sunbeds; consider evening dosing only where evidence supports it (e.g. some advise doxycycline with evening meal — mixed evidence; protection remains essential).
Report suspected ADRs via **MHRA Yellow Card** (serious, novel, or black-triangle drugs).

management: Blistering over large area, mucosal involvement or systemic illness (consider SJS/TEN, not photosensitivity) → **same-day**; persistent eruption after stopping drug (persistent light reaction/CAD) → dermatology; lupus-like eruption → GP bloods/dermatology; **voriconazole long-term + photodamage** → dermatology for skin cancer surveillance.

management.h: Photosensitiser drug checklist for medication review

management: Paraphrased from DermNet and BNF photosensitivity side-effect listings; **always check the current BNF monograph and SmPC** for an individual drug. = commonest/most important in UK primary care.

head: Class
Examples (UK-relevant)
Main type / notes
rows: Phototoxic; photo-onycholysis; pseudoporphyria. Counsel every supply (acne, rosacea, malaria prophylaxis)
ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin; nalidixic acid
**voriconazole** (also SCC/melanoma risk), griseofulvin, itraconazole/ketoconazole (rare), terbinafine (drug-induced SCLE)
**topical ketoprofen** (photoallergy — avoid sun on site during + 2 weeks after), piroxicam, naproxen (pseudoporphyria), ibuprofen (rare), diclofenac, celecoxib
**thiazides/related** (bendroflumethiazide, hydrochlorothiazide — MHRA NMSC risk, indapamide, chlortalidone), furosemide, bumetanide (pseudoporphyria)

**amiodarone** (phototoxic, blue-grey pigmentation; persists months), dronedarone, quinidine; calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine, diltiazem — photo-distributed telangiectasia/pigmentation), ACE inhibitors (rare), statins (rare)
Do not stop amiodarone without cardiology
chlorpromazine and other phenothiazines (incl. topical promethazine), tricyclic antidepressants, St John's wort (hypericin)
quinine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine (paradoxically treats some photodermatoses), mefloquine (rare)
methotrexate (UV recall), fluorouracil (systemic/topical), vemurafenib (marked UVA phototoxicity), BRAF/MEK & checkpoint inhibitors, hydroxycarbamide
sunscreen filters (oxybenzone, octocrylene), fragrances, coal tar, benzoyl peroxide (irritant)

red_flags: Blistering, extensive or systemic reaction: same-day assessment.
Long-term voriconazole with photodamage: monitor for skin cancer.
pearls: Always ask **"any new tablets, creams or herbal remedies in the last 3 months?"** for any photo-distributed rash.

**Doxycycline** (acne, rosacea, malaria prophylaxis, Lyme, chest infections) — the commonest UK primary-care culprit; give the sun advice **with every supply**, especially malaria prophylaxis for sunny destinations.

**Topical ketoprofen gel** — BNF/MHRA advice: avoid exposure of treated area to sunlight/UV (incl. sunbeds) **during treatment and for 2 weeks after**, wash hands, avoid octocrylene-containing sunscreens/fragrance co-sensitisers.

**Hydrochlorothiazide** — MHRA (2018) Drug Safety Update: cumulative-dose-related increased risk of **non-melanoma skin cancer**; advise sun protection, skin checks, and review in those with prior skin cancer. (Bendroflumethiazide is the usual UK thiazide; photosensitivity also listed.)
**Voriconazole** — phototoxicity and **squamous cell carcinoma/melanoma** risk with long-term use (MHRA warning): strict photoprotection; dermatology review.
**Fluoroquinolones** — photosensitivity listed; MHRA restrictions on use for other safety reasons; avoid strong sun/sunbeds during and for a few days after.
**Isotretinoin/acitretin** — increased sunburn/skin fragility (retinoid effect, not classic phototoxicity).
Check the **BNF monograph side-effects / "Patient and carer advice"** for photosensitivity statements — the definitive UK source for counselling labels.
